venue_now: Text shows 'Preprint. Under review.' and arXiv:2504.16074v2, 18 May 2025 (p.1). cited_set_resolution.md lists NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (poster).
what_it_is: A physics reasoning benchmark of 500 problems from high-school to Physics Olympiad level whose answers are single symbolic expressions (p.1, pp.3-4). The problems were adapted from exercises for human learners by 178 Peking University physics students, drawn from non-public and public sources not easily found online, reviewed by experts, and filtered after 81 students (50 Chinese Physics Olympiad gold medallists) attempted them, keeping 500 of 757 (pp.4-5). Answers are scored by binary symbolic equivalence and by the EED Score, a model-free expression-tree edit distance that gives partial credit (pp.5-6). Across 16 models the best, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reaches 36.9% accuracy against a human baseline of 61.9% (p.1, p.6).
domain: physics, high school to olympiad: mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, optics, modern physics, advanced physics (p.2, p.3)
size: 500 problems; 16 models (14 by API, 2 locally), some at several reasoning-effort settings (p.6; 19 bars in Figure 1, p.2); human baseline from 81 students and 559 answer sheets (p.6)
source_of_items: expert-written: adapted from exercises designed for human learners (non-public and public sources not easily found online) by 178 physics students, then expert-reviewed (pp.4-5)
has_gold_traces: partial: reference solutions exist (a full solution averages about 3,000 characters, p.27) and are used in the chain-of-thought poisoning experiment (p.27), but scoring uses only the final expression (p.10, p.20)
evaluation: final answer, expression-level metric: binary accuracy by SymPy equivalence (p.17) and the EED Score (relative tree edit distance r between gold and model expressions: 100 for an exact match, 60 - 100r for 0 < r < 0.6, else 0) (pp.5-6)
human_validation: 178 contributors; each question checked by expert reviewers, who were shown LLM outputs to spot ambiguity; 81 students (50 CPhO gold medallists) attempted subsets and gave feedback, leaving 500 of 757 questions (66.1%) (pp.4-5); human baseline 61.9 +/- 2.1% accuracy and 70.4 +/- 1.8 EED (p.6). I found no check of the EED or accuracy scorer against human grading and no agreement statistic.
contamination_measures: original or adapted problems from sources 'none of which are easily discoverable through direct internet search or standard references' (p.4); the paper says this eliminates contamination (p.2), but the problems are adapted from existing exercises (p.4) and the dataset is public (p.1)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-P1 (L172-177): '... others target advanced symbolic (Zhang et al., 2025b; Qiu et al., 2025) or qualitative (Wang et al., 2023; Shojaee et al., 2025) understanding.' S-P2 (L177-180, uncited, covers all six): 'Despite this progress, these benchmarks remain confined to theoretical physics, lacking the integrative context of engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: The gist holds: answers must be single symbolic expressions (p.4) scored by a symbolic-expression metric (p.3, p.5), and the problems run up to olympiad level (p.1). But the paper's stated target is 'physical perception and robust reasoning' (p.2), and its own error analysis puts over 90% of reasoning errors in semantic rather than symbolic reasoning (p.8), so 'symbolic understanding' describes the answer format more than the construct. S-P2's 'theoretical physics' is loose: the paper presents 'realistic physical scenarios' from high-school to olympiad physics (p.4). The closing 'outcome matching' sentence (L199-201) is accurate for PHYBench, which says the EED Score 'focuses on final answer quality and does not capture the full reasoning process' (p.10), though EED gives partial credit rather than an exact match.

suggested_wording: PHYBench (Qiu et al., 2025) adapts 500 high-school to olympiad physics problems so that they cannot easily be found online and scores the final symbolic expression with a tree edit distance that gives partial credit, noting that this does not assess the reasoning process.
facts_to_cite: 500 physics problems from high-school to Physics Olympiad level, each answered by a single symbolic expression (p.1, p.4)

Adapted from exercises for human learners by 178 Peking University physics students, from sources not easily found by internet search; 500 kept of 757 after 81 students (50 CPhO gold medallists) attempted them (pp.4-5)
Scored by symbolic equivalence and by the EED Score, a model-free tree edit distance over SymPy expression trees with partial credit (pp.5-6)
Best model Gemini 2.5 Pro: 36.9% accuracy, against a human baseline of 61.9% (p.1, p.6)

The authors state that the EED Score focuses on final-answer quality and does not capture the reasoning process, and that non-unique solution paths make a single canonical trace hard to define (p.10, p.20)

In a first-mistake analysis of traces from seven models on 50 problems, over 90% of errors arise after the physical scenario is correctly understood, and over 90% of those are semantic rather than symbolic (p.8)
A chain-of-thought poisoning experiment injects errors into truncated reference solutions and checks whether models detect them (pp.8-9, p.27)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: multi-step quantitative physics problems; careful human curation with a human baseline; an analysis that injects errors into partial solutions (pp.8-9, p.27), comparable in spirit to EngTrace's planted defects; it names the problem EngTrace's order-free milestones address, that solution paths are non-unique so a single canonical trace is hard to define (p.20). Lacks: generated instances (500 fixed problems, publicly released, which limits its contamination argument); gold traces in scoring; step-level evaluation (stated as a limitation, p.10); an engineering domain; validation of its scorer against human grading. EngTrace lacks its human baseline.
notes: PHYBench proposes physics-informed checks such as unit or dimensional analysis as future work for its metric (p.20). 'Original' in the paper means adapted rather than newly invented (p.4); do not repeat the paper's claim that it eliminates contamination, say instead that the problems were chosen not to be easily found online. Reference-list error (confirmed on p.1): printed 'Siyu Qiu, Shuo Guo, Ze-Yu Song, et al.'; the first three authors are Shi Qiu, Shaoyang Guo, Zhuo-Yang Song. ABench-Physics cites PHYBench twice (its 2025a and 2025b entries), which is the source of its contrast with expression answers.
